explain.body: Computational thinking is a problem-solving process. It uses a set of skills and techniques to solve complex problems in a way that can be executed by a computer. It can also help with problems in everyday life and fields beyond computer science.

explain.title: Decomposition and pattern recognition
explain.body: Decomposition divides a complex problem into smaller, manageable tasks. Pattern recognition looks for similarities or regularities among and within problems. For example, square areas follow the sums of consecutive odd numbers: 1, 1 + 3, 1 + 3 + 5, and so on.

explain.title: Abstraction
explain.body: Abstraction is the process of hiding the complex details while exposing only the necessary parts. This reduces complexity and lets us focus on the high-level overview. For making tea, the high-level steps are to boil water, add tea, steep it, and pour it into a cup.

explain.title: Algorithms

writtenQuestions.text: Pseudocode for determining if a number is prime.
modelAnswer: Procedure Is Prime(number)
Input: number {The number to be checked}
Output: True if number is prime, False otherwise

if (number <= 1) then
return False
end if
for i from 2 to sqrt(number) do
if (number % i == 0) then
return False
end if
end for
return True
End

explain.title: Flowcharts
explain.body: Flowcharts are visual representations of the steps in a process or system, depicted using different symbols connected by arrows. They help people see a process and its decisions clearly.

explain.title: Flowchart symbols
explain.body: An oval represents the start or end. A rectangle represents a process or task. A parallelogram represents input or output. A diamond represents a decision. An arrow, or flowline, shows the direction of flow.

explain.title: Pseudocode
explain.body: Pseudocode is a method of representing an algorithm using simple and informal language that is easy to understand. It is not actual code that can be run on a computer; it helps you focus on the algorithm's logic without worrying about programming syntax.

explain.title: Choosing a method
explain.body: Flowcharts show the flow visually, which helps you see the overall structure and decisions. Pseudocode describes each step in a structured, readable way and is useful when planning how to turn an algorithm into code.

explain.title: Decisions in algorithms
explain.body: A decision checks a condition and chooses a path. In a flowchart, the decision is shown with a diamond and branches such as Yes and No. In pseudocode, the decision can be written with if, then, else, and End if.

explain.title: Big O notation

explain.title: Space complexity

explain.title: Three types of errors
explain.body: Syntax Errors: These occur when we write something incorrectly in our algorithm or flowchart. For example, missing a step or using the wrong symbol. Runtime Errors: These happen when the algorithm or flowchart is being executed. For example, trying to perform an impossible operation, such as dividing by zero. Logical Errors: These are mistakes in the logic of the algorithm that cause it to behave incorrectly. For example, using the wrong condition in a decision step.

explain.title: Debugging
explain.body: Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in an algorithm or flowchart. Syntax errors are often easiest to find because LARP usually points them out. Logical errors can be harder because the algorithm may still run but produce incorrect results.

explain.title: Debugging techniques

Simplify the Problem: Break down the algorithm into smaller parts and test each part separately.

explain.title: Common LARP error messages
explain.body: Missing Step means you probably forgot an important step. Undefined Variable means you are using a variable that has not been defined yet. Invalid Operation means you are trying to perform an operation that is not allowed, like dividing by zero.

explain.title: Computational thinking
explain.body: Computational thinking is a systematic, algorithmic, and logical approach to solving problems. It is useful beyond programming because many real-world tasks can be organised and solved in steps.

explain.title: Decomposition and pattern recognition
explain.body: Decomposition breaks a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts. Pattern recognition finds similarities or repeated features, so useful steps or solutions can be reused.

explain.title: Abstraction
explain.body: Abstraction ignores unnecessary details and focuses on the main idea or information needed for the task. This makes a complex problem simpler to understand and solve.

explain.title: Algorithms and their representations
explain.body: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. A flowchart represents an algorithm graphically with symbols and arrows; pseudocode describes its steps in structured plain language.

explain.title: Dry runs, debugging, and LARP
explain.body: A dry run traces an algorithm with sample data to check its steps and results. Debugging finds and corrects errors. LARP supports learning algorithms through logic and reasoning practice.

mistakes: Do not define computational thinking as programming alone; it is a problem-solving approach.
Do not confuse decomposition (breaking a problem into parts) with abstraction (ignoring irrelevant details).
In a grade algorithm, check thresholds from highest to lowest so that each mark receives the correct grade.
Do not leave out the otherwise case; every possible input should have a result.
Do not call pseudocode a programming language; it describes an algorithm in plain language.
A dry run means tracing steps with sample data, not writing or executing program code.

notes.title: Computational Thinking: Four Useful Tools
notes.answer: Computational thinking is a problem-solving process that uses skills such as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithms.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking is a way to work through complex problems so that the solution can be carried out by a computer. Its four key components are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithms.
notes.simple: Think of computational thinking as a problem-solving toolkit: split a big task into parts, notice patterns, ignore details that do not matter, and follow clear steps.
examples: To build a birdhouse, split the task into designing it, gathering materials, cutting the wood, assembling the pieces, decorating it, and installing it.
The areas of squares with sides 1, 2, and 3 are 1, 4, and 9. These are also the sums 1, 1 + 3, and 1 + 3 + 5.
steps: Understand the problem and what needs to be done.
Use decomposition to divide a complex task into smaller tasks.
Use pattern recognition to spot similarities or regularities.
Use abstraction to focus on necessary details and leave out unnecessary ones.
Write an algorithm: a precise sequence of instructions to reach the goal.
notes.checkAnswer: Decomposition means breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts.

notes.title: Principles of Computational Thinking
notes.answer: The three principles in this section are problem understanding, problem simplification, and solution selection and design.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking starts by understanding the problem, then simplifying it into manageable parts, and choosing and planning a suitable solution.
notes.simple: First understand what needs to be done. Then divide the work into smaller parts and plan a suitable way to complete them.
examples: Before building a school website, find out what pages it needs, who will use it, and what tools are available.
To design a website, split the work into layout, content, and functionality.
steps: Understand the problem and identify its requirements.
Set clear objectives for the outcome.
Break a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
Evaluate possible approaches and select an efficient solution.
Create a detailed plan or algorithm for the solution.
notes.checkAnswer: Break the problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.

notes.title: Choosing an Algorithm Design Method
notes.answer: Flowcharts and pseudocode are two ways to describe an algorithm. Flowcharts use graphical symbols and arrows. Pseudocode uses plain language and a structured format.
notes.explanation: Flowcharts show an algorithm with symbols and arrows; pseudocode describes its steps in simple, structured language. Use the method that makes the algorithm easiest to understand and check.
notes.simple: A flowchart is a picture of the steps. Pseudocode is a written plan of the steps.
examples: A flowchart uses a diamond for a decision such as “Is the item available?”
Pseudocode can use if/else to print “Even” or “Odd”.
steps: Identify the steps and decisions needed to solve the problem.
Use a flowchart when you want to show the overall flow visually.
Use pseudocode when you want to describe the logic step by step in words.
Check that each decision has the correct branches and that the process can reach an end.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one main difference between a flowchart and pseudocode?
notes.checkAnswer: A flowchart is visual and uses symbols and arrows; pseudocode uses plain language in a structured format.

notes.title: Checking how algorithms work
notes.answer: A dry run checks an algorithm step by step using sample data.
notes.explanation: Time complexity describes how an algorithm’s running time changes as the input gets bigger. Space complexity describes how much memory it uses. Dry runs and simulations help check that an algorithm works as intended.
notes.simple: Time complexity is about time and steps; space complexity is about memory. A dry run is a careful test using sample data.
examples: If you check each name in a list one by one, a longer list may take more steps.
A dry run uses sample data to check an algorithm without actually running a program.
steps: Choose sample input data.
Follow the algorithm one step at a time.
Keep track of the values and actions at each step.
Check whether the result is correct.

notes.answer: A dry run involves manually going through the algorithm with sample data to identify any errors.
notes.explanation: A dry run means following an algorithm manually with sample data. You track what happens at each step, including the values of variables and the output. This can help you spot logic errors before using a computer.

notes.title: Practising algorithms with LARP
notes.answer: LARP stands for Logic of Algorithms for resolution of Problems. It lets learners run algorithms and observe their results.
notes.explanation: LARP is a tool for trying out algorithms: you provide inputs, run the instructions, and observe the outputs. It uses simple commands such as START, READ, WRITE, IF...THEN...ELSE, and END.
notes.simple: LARP is like a practice space where you can run an algorithm and see what it does.
examples: An even-or-odd algorithm reads a number and displays whether it is even or odd.
A salary algorithm can calculate annual salary and display whether tax applies.
steps: Start the algorithm with START.
Use READ to get input and WRITE to display messages or results.
Use IF...THEN...ELSE when the algorithm must make a decision.
Finish the algorithm with END.
Run the algorithm with different inputs and check its outputs.

notes.title: Error Identification and Debugging
notes.answer: Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in an algorithm or flowchart.
notes.explanation: Algorithms and flowcharts can contain errors, or bugs. Debugging means finding and fixing them. You can trace the steps, use comments, check decision conditions, and test smaller parts separately.
notes.simple: Debugging is checking an algorithm to find what is wrong and then fixing it.
examples: If an algorithm tries to divide by zero while it runs, that is a runtime error.
If a decision uses the wrong condition and gives the wrong result, that is a logical error.
steps: Read any error message carefully.
Trace the algorithm step by step with sample data.
Check that decision conditions are correct.
Use comments to clarify what each part should do.
Break the problem into smaller parts and test them separately.

notes.title: Computational Thinking: Solve Problems Step by Step
notes.answer: Computational thinking is a systematic, logical approach to understanding and solving problems. It uses decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking is a way to solve problems systematically. It includes understanding the problem, breaking it into parts, finding patterns, focusing on important details, and designing and checking a solution.
notes.simple: Computational thinking means working out a problem carefully, in manageable steps, before or while using a computer.
examples: A recipe gives ordered instructions for preparing food, much like an algorithm.
A school timetable can be simplified by focusing on each class's time and room, rather than every detail about the school.
steps: Understand what the problem asks and identify the information you need.
Decompose the problem into smaller parts.
Look for similarities or repeated steps (patterns).
Ignore unnecessary details and focus on what matters (abstraction).
Design a step-by-step algorithm, using pseudocode or a flowchart if helpful.
Dry run the solution with sample data and debug any errors.

quiz.stem: What does space complexity help us evaluate?

quiz.stem: What does it mean to dry run an algorithm?

Manually follow the algorithm using sample data
Change the algorithm without checking it
Draw only the input and output symbols

quiz.stem: Which statement is NOT given as a benefit of simulation in this section?

quiz.stem: An algorithm runs without stopping, but produces the wrong result because it uses an incorrect decision condition. What kind of error is this?

Runtime error
Logical error
Missing comment

Use only larger test problems.

An undefined variable

Remove all input values from the algorithm.

quiz.stem: Q7.5. Which of the following is a principle of computational thinking?
options: Ignoring problem understanding
Problem simplification
Avoiding solution design
Implementing random solutions

Repetitive patterns

Understanding the problem
Designing a flowchart
Selecting a solution

Solve mathematical equations

quiz.stem: Q7.9. Pseudocode is:

written.text: Q7.4. Discuss the concept of decomposition in computational thinking. Why is it important?
modelAnswer: Decomposition is the process of breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable parts.
Each part can be understood and solved separately, which makes the whole problem less difficult.
The parts can be tested individually and then combined to form the complete solution.
For example, planning a school event can be decomposed into arranging a venue, preparing a schedule, inviting participants, and organising equipment.
Each task can be assigned and checked separately, making the event easier to plan successfully.

written.text: Q7.5. Explain pattern recognition in the context of computational thinking. How does identifying patterns help in problem-solving?
modelAnswer: Pattern recognition in computational thinking is finding and using similarities or repeated features within problems.
When a pattern is recognised, a known solution or set of steps may be reused, reducing effort and helping predict what will happen.
For example, if several school forms require the same basic information, the repeated fields can be identified and handled using the same procedure.
Recognising such patterns makes it easier to design a consistent solution rather than solving each similar task from the beginning.

written.text: Q7.6. What is an abstraction in computational thinking? Discuss its importance and provide examples of how abstraction can be used to simplify complex problems.
modelAnswer: Abstraction in computational thinking means ignoring unnecessary details and focusing on the main idea or relevant information.
It is important because it reduces complexity and helps us concentrate on the information needed to solve a problem.
For example, a route map shows roads and destinations needed to choose a journey, while leaving out details such as the colour of buildings.
The map is therefore a simpler representation suited to the task of finding a route.

written.text: Q7.9. Explain the concept of a dry run in the context of both flowcharts and pseudocode. How does performing a dry run help in validating the correctness of an algorithm?
modelAnswer: A dry run is the manual tracing of an algorithm's steps using sample data.
For a flowchart, follow the arrows and symbols; for pseudocode, follow each instruction in order.
Record the values and decisions as the sample input passes through the algorithm.
Compare the final output with the expected result.
If the output is incorrect, the trace helps locate the step or decision causing the error, so the algorithm can be debugged before implementation.

written.text: Q7.10. What is LARP? Discuss its importance in learning and practicing algorithms.
modelAnswer: LARP means Logic And Reasoning Process and is used to learn and practise algorithmic thinking.
It helps learners follow an algorithm's steps and reason about the decisions it makes.
By working through an algorithm, learners can check how inputs lead to outputs and identify errors in the logic.
This practice builds understanding before the algorithm is implemented in a computer program.
